Amina Adebayo is a young woman living alone in a rented room in Mushin, Lagos. Every Friday evening she oils the hinges of the box, a ritual her father taught her: a tool that is kept is a tool that lasts. She budgets meticulously, recording every expense—50 naira for water, 100 for groundnuts, 200 for a notebook leaf—in a notebook written in careful English. She does not laugh easily but has smiled privately at a fellow trainee, Emeka, a quiet older man who sometimes shares his offcuts with her and has become a silent ally in the workshop.

Amina would need to miss her afternoon carpentry class and pay for transport to Ibadan. She has only a few days to reply. Her mother writes that she can borrow a lace blouse from her sister.
